e-7400.knowledge_point: Creating an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Polar Curve
e-7400.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/e5647c0f19727d1e626e637464cc57444e0bc0f2f8e99a4afd15d3c3631dc3f0.png)

Find an integral expression for the arc length of the polar curve $r=3-\sin(7\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi,$ shown in blue in the diagram above.
e-7400.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ is given by

$$
L =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=3-\sin(7\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} =-7\cos(7\theta)
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(3-\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta ))^{2}+(-7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+49{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+1+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{10-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

e-641.knowledge_point: Finding the Arc Length of a Polar Curve
e-641.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/0bb9e5e7315d4bcd5fc21700fdd2597f6d9b585a109145de53c6f94e9530eabf.png)

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2(1-\cos\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ (shown in blue in the picture above).
e-641.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ is given by

$$
L =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=2(1-\cos\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 2\sin\theta.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now use the half-angle formula $1-\cos\theta =2\sin^2\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={-4\cdot 2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-8(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-8(0-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=2cos⁡(3θ) for −π6≤θ≤π6?

a
2∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
b
∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
c
∫0π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+3sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
d
2∫0π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
e
2∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+3sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Polar arc length is L=∫√(r²+(dr/dθ)²) dθ. Since dr/dθ=-6sin(3θ), the integrand is √(4cos²(3θ)+36sin²(3θ))=2√(cos²(3θ)+9sin²(3θ)). Using the stated bounds gives option a.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}?$
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}+(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+36{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta ))}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=2cos⁡(3θ) for −π6≤θ≤π6?

a
2∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
b
∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
c
∫0π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+3sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
d
2∫0π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
e
2∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+3sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=2cos⁡(3θ), we have drdθ=−6sin⁡(3θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/6π/6(2cos⁡(3θ))2+(−6sin⁡(3θ))2dθ=∫−π/6π/64cos2⁡(3θ)+36sin2⁡(3θ)dθ=∫−π/6π/64(cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ))dθ=2∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ.

content.knowledge_point: Creating an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Polar Curve
content.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}?$
content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}+(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+36{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta ))}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=3sin⁡(4θ) for 0≤θ≤π4 (shown in blue in the diagram above)?

a
3∫0π/4sin2⁡(4θ)+16cos2⁡(4θ)dθ
b
32∫0π/4sin2⁡(4θ)+16cos2⁡(4θ)dθ
c
3∫0π/4sin2⁡(4θ)+4cos2⁡(4θ)dθ
d
∫0π/4sin2⁡(4θ)+4cos2⁡(4θ)dθ
e
12∫0π/4sin2⁡(4θ)+4cos2⁡(4θ)dθ
Submit

decision.explanation: For a polar curve, L=∫√(r²+(dr/dθ)²) dθ. Here dr/dθ=12cos(4θ), so √(r²+(dr/dθ)²)=√(9sin²(4θ)+144cos²(4θ))=3√(sin²(4θ)+16cos²(4θ)). Integrating from 0 to π/4 gives option a.

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=12\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ))^{2}+(12\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡(4\theta )+144{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡(4\theta )+16{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta ))}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(4\theta )+16{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=3sin⁡(4θ) for 0≤θ≤π4 (shown in blue in the diagram above)?

a
3∫0π/4sin2⁡(4θ)+16cos2⁡(4θ)dθ
b
32∫0π/4sin2⁡(4θ)+16cos2⁡(4θ)dθ
c
3∫0π/4sin2⁡(4θ)+4cos2⁡(4θ)dθ
d
∫0π/4sin2⁡(4θ)+4cos2⁡(4θ)dθ
e
12∫0π/4sin2⁡(4θ)+4cos2⁡(4θ)dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=3sin⁡(4θ), we have

drdθ=12cos⁡(4θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/4(3sin⁡(4θ))2+(12cos⁡(4θ))2dθ=∫0π/49sin2⁡(4θ)+144cos2⁡(4θ)dθ=∫0π/49(sin2⁡(4θ)+16cos2⁡(4θ))dθ=3∫0π/4sin2⁡(4θ)+16cos2⁡(4θ)dθ.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a: dr/dθ=12cos(4θ), so √(r²+(dr/dθ)²)=3√(sin²(4θ)+16cos²(4θ)). The deliberately submitted option c has 4 instead of 16 and is incorrect.

content.knowledge_point: Creating an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Polar Curve
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/3a760f55b6437a39010e4d1a00bdb5fb5390d848dd74347e7736e2ac49cd562b.png)

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=12\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ))^{2}+(12\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡(4\theta )+144{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡(4\theta )+16{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta ))}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(4\theta )+16{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=3−cos⁡(3θ) for 0≤θ≤π2 (shown in blue in the diagram above).

a
∫0π/210−6cos⁡(3θ)+8cos2⁡(3θ)dθ
b
∫0π/210−3cos⁡(3θ)+8cos2⁡(3θ)dθ
c
∫0π/210−6cos⁡(3θ)+8sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
d
∫0π/29−6cos⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
e
∫0π/29−3cos⁡(3θ)+8sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Polar arc length is ∫√(r²+(dr/dθ)²) dθ. Here dr/dθ=3sin(3θ), giving r²+(dr/dθ)²=9−6cos(3θ)+cos²(3θ)+9sin²(3θ)=10−6cos(3θ)+8sin²(3θ). Thus option c is correct.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/59214bcbfd4b1d718faa0c2355e932ab3cedae5b785b17497cef554ee3ec099b.png)

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=3-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above).
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(3-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+1+8{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{10-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+8{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=3−cos⁡(3θ) for 0≤θ≤π2 (shown in blue in the diagram above).

a
∫0π/210−6cos⁡(3θ)+8cos2⁡(3θ)dθ
b
∫0π/210−3cos⁡(3θ)+8cos2⁡(3θ)dθ
c
∫0π/210−6cos⁡(3θ)+8sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
d
∫0π/29−6cos⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
e
∫0π/29−3cos⁡(3θ)+8sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=3−cos⁡(3θ), we have drdθ=3sin⁡(3θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/2(3−cos⁡(3θ))2+(3sin⁡(3θ))2dθ=∫0π/29−6cos⁡(3θ)+cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ=∫0π/29−6cos⁡(3θ)+1+8sin2⁡(3θ)dθ=∫0π/210−6cos⁡(3θ)+8sin2⁡(3θ)dθ.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/59214bcbfd4b1d718faa0c2355e932ab3cedae5b785b17497cef554ee3ec099b.png)

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=3-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above).
content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(3-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+1+8{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{10-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+8{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=4cos⁡(3θ) for π2≤θ≤5π6 (shown in blue in the diagram above)?

a
43∫π/25π/6sin2⁡(3θ)+9cos2⁡(3θ)dθ
b
34∫π/25π/6sin2⁡(3θ)+cos2⁡(3θ)dθ
c
4∫π/25π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
d
4∫π/25π/6cos2⁡(3θ)−sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
e
3∫π/25π/6cos2⁡(3θ)−3sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Polar arc length is ∫√(r²+(dr/dθ)²) dθ. Since dr/dθ=−12sin(3θ), the integrand is √(16cos²(3θ)+144sin²(3θ))=4√(cos²(3θ)+9sin²(3θ)). With the given bounds, this is option c.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/b1a0f5b8438b5abeafafccadd5a3a33572441c4d58d2e97f7254bd28987c223c.png)

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{5\pi }{6}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}+(-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+144{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{16({cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta ))}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=4cos⁡(3θ) for π2≤θ≤5π6 (shown in blue in the diagram above)?

a
43∫π/25π/6sin2⁡(3θ)+9cos2⁡(3θ)dθ
b
34∫π/25π/6sin2⁡(3θ)+cos2⁡(3θ)dθ
c
4∫π/25π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
d
4∫π/25π/6cos2⁡(3θ)−sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
e
3∫π/25π/6cos2⁡(3θ)−3sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=4cos⁡(3θ), we have

drdθ=−12sin⁡(3θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫π/25π/6(4cos⁡(3θ))2+(−12sin⁡(3θ))2dθ=∫π/25π/616cos2⁡(3θ)+144sin2⁡(3θ)dθ=∫π/25π/616(cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ))dθ=4∫π/25π/6cos2⁡(3θ)+9sin2⁡(3θ)dθ.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option c. Since dr/dθ=−12sin(3θ), the arc-length integrand is √(16cos²(3θ)+144sin²(3θ))=4√(cos²(3θ)+9sin²(3θ)). The deliberately submitted option a is incorrect.

content.knowledge_point: Creating an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Polar Curve
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/b1a0f5b8438b5abeafafccadd5a3a33572441c4d58d2e97f7254bd28987c223c.png)

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{5\pi }{6}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}+(-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+144{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{16({cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta ))}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following integrals gives the arc length of the polar curve r=1+sin⁡(2θ) for −π4≤θ≤π4 (shown in blue in the diagram above)?

a
∫0π/21+2sin⁡(2θ)+4cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
b
∫0π/22+2sin⁡(2θ)+3cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
c
∫−π/4π/42+2sin⁡(2θ)+3cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
d
∫−π/4π/42+4sin⁡(2θ)+2cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
e
∫−π/4π/41+2sin⁡(2θ)+4cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Using L=∫√(r²+(dr/dθ)²) dθ and dr/dθ=2cos(2θ), the radicand is (1+sin(2θ))²+4cos²(2θ)=2+2sin(2θ)+3cos²(2θ). With bounds −π/4 to π/4, this gives option c.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/00e5e0f5c47a056beaca2d7bc1b1d10a6a11f96398df7400e69c023f5780b8a6.png)

Which of the following integrals gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$ for $-\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}$ (shown in blue in the  diagram above)?
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )+4{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+1+3{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+3{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following integrals gives the arc length of the polar curve r=1+sin⁡(2θ) for −π4≤θ≤π4 (shown in blue in the diagram above)?

a
∫0π/21+2sin⁡(2θ)+4cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
b
∫0π/22+2sin⁡(2θ)+3cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
c
∫−π/4π/42+2sin⁡(2θ)+3cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
d
∫−π/4π/42+4sin⁡(2θ)+2cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
e
∫−π/4π/41+2sin⁡(2θ)+4cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=1+sin⁡(2θ), we have

drdθ=2cos⁡(2θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/4π/4(1+sin⁡(2θ))2+(2cos⁡(2θ))2dθ=∫−π/4π/41+2sin⁡(2θ)+sin2⁡(2θ)+4cos2⁡(2θ)dθ=∫−π/4π/41+2sin⁡(2θ)+1+3cos2⁡(2θ)dθ=∫−π/4π/42+2sin⁡(2θ)+3cos2⁡(2θ)dθ.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/00e5e0f5c47a056beaca2d7bc1b1d10a6a11f96398df7400e69c023f5780b8a6.png)

Which of the following integrals gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$ for $-\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}$ (shown in blue in the  diagram above)?
content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )+4{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+1+3{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+3{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since r=3e^θ and dr/dθ=3e^θ, the arc length is ∫₀^{π/4}√(9e^{2θ}+9e^{2θ}) dθ=3√2∫₀^{π/4}e^θ dθ=3√2(e^{π/4}−1). Thus option d is correct.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/fa1c1c3ae2769f45854de4f0b00fc394fccb40b40704cfd09e6eb11eee3c07af.png)

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=3{e}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above).
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3{e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(3{e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{(3{e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9{e}^{2\theta }+9{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{18{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{e}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /4}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =3\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Find the arc length of the polar curve r=3eθ for 0≤θ≤π4 (shown in blue in the diagram above).

a
3eπ/4
b
2eπ/4−1
c
2(eπ/4−1)
d
32(eπ/4−1)
e
32(eπ/4−e−π/4)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=3eθ, we have drdθ=3eθ.

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/4(3eθ)2+(3eθ)2dθ=∫0π/49e2θ+9e2θdθ=∫0π/418e2θdθ=32∫0π/4eθdθ=32eθ|0π/4=32(eπ/4−e0)=32(eπ/4−1).

decision.explanation: Since dr/dθ=−2sin(θ), the arc-length integrand is √((2+2cos(θ))²+4sin²(θ))=√(8+8cos(θ))=4cos(θ/2) on [0,π]. Thus L=∫₀^π4cos(θ/2) dθ=[8sin(θ/2)]₀^π=8, giving option e.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/3387790df770ac8645058c6f460b1f1285629d18d765668e362a8070ae4035ed.png)

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi $ (shown in blue in the diagram above).

*Hint: You may wish to use the following identity: $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}.$*
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{8}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the identity for $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}):$

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}
$$

Therefore, using $x=\theta $ in the previous identity, the integral can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={4\cdot 2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =8(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi $ (shown in blue in the diagram above).

*Hint: You may wish to use the following identity: $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}.$*
content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{8}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the identity for $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}):$

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}
$$

Therefore, using $x=\theta $ in the previous identity, the integral can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={4\cdot 2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =8(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{7\pi /4}\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{7\pi /4}\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{7\pi /4}1\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\theta {|}_{3\pi /2}^{7\pi /4} \\  & =2(\frac{7\pi }{4}-\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
